lead: Every editing tool answers one question first: does it store a grid of pixels, or a list of objects? Paint tools change pixels, so the picture is frozen at the resolution it was made. Drawing tools store shapes you can re-edit, so they stay sharp at any zoom. Image editing tools act on the whole picture — crop, resample, colour shift. That one storage choice fixes resolution, editing power and file size, and it separates the tool families in an authoring package: painting, drawing, image editing, 3D modelling, animation, audio and movie tools.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 on raster versus vector graphics and colour models, and Unit 4 on image file formats.

sections.h3: Paint tools write into the pixel grid

blocks.text: A paint program keeps a canvas, which is a grid of pixels. A brush of diameter d pixels stamps colour into every pixel its path touches, so a soft edge is really a row of partly transparent pixels. An airbrush sprays with a density setting: repeated passes build up opacity. An eraser writes the background colour, or alpha 0 on a transparent canvas. Bucket fill floods the connected region of pixels whose colour lies within a tolerance of the clicked pixel; a small tolerance leaves a halo at anti-aliased edges.

Any shape drawn in a paint program — rectangle, ellipse, text — is rendered into the bitmap the moment you release the mouse. Its corner radius cannot be changed afterwards. The file is a bitmap, so its uncompressed size depends only on width, height and bit depth, and its resolution is fixed when the canvas is created.

A drawing program stores each object as numbers: the endpoints of a line, the centre and radii of an ellipse, the anchors of a curve, plus a stroke colour, a stroke width and a fill colour. Nothing becomes pixels until the picture is displayed or exported. Move a node, change a fill, scale the drawing up to a banner — the software re-renders from the same numbers and the edges stay clean. A 20 mm circle on a poster and the same circle on a phone screen are one object with two renderings. Paths and the pen tool are covered in 5.8.
A pixel-based image editor works on a photograph or a finished bitmap. You select a region — rectangle, lasso, or magic wand by colour similarity — then apply one operation.
Crop keeps the selected rectangle and discards the rest. The pixel count falls, the dots per inch (dpi) value stays, so the printed size shrinks.

Resample changes the number of pixels. Downsampling throws pixels away. Upsampling must invent them by interpolation: nearest neighbour copies the closest pixel and looks blocky, bilinear averages four neighbours and looks soft, bicubic fits a smooth surface and keeps edges crisper. Resize keeps the pixel count and changes only the print size, which changes the dpi.

blocks.where: S is the uncompressed size in bytes; W and H are the pixel width and height; b is the bit depth, equal to 24 for 8-bit RGB and 8 for greyscale or an indexed palette.

blocks.text: Bit depth sets how many values a channel can take: 8 bits give 256 levels, so 24-bit RGB gives 16,777,216 colours, and an 8-bit indexed image holds one of 256 palette entries per pixel. Brightness adds a constant to every channel. Contrast scales values away from mid-grey. A hue shift rotates the hue angle θ in HSV, which is how a red shirt turns blue without touching saturation.

examples.question: An image is 4 in × 4 in at 300 dpi in 24-bit colour. Find its pixel dimensions and its uncompressed size in bytes and megabytes. Then find the pixel dimensions and size after resampling to 150 dpi at the same print size.
steps: Pixels per side = 4 in × 300 dpi = 1200 px, because dpi is pixels per inch.
Uncompressed size = 1,440,000 × 3 B = 4,320,000 B = 4.32 MB, taking 1 MB = 10⁶ B.
Resampled pixels = 600 × 600 = 360,000 px, one quarter of the original.
examples.answer: The image is 1200 × 1200 px and 4,320,000 B (4.32 MB); after resampling to 150 dpi it is 600 × 600 px and 1,080,000 B (1.08 MB).
examples.check:
size_in = 4
dpi = 300
bpp = 24
px = size_in * dpi
total = px * px
bytes_full = total * bpp // 8
new_dpi = 150
px2 = size_in * new_dpi
total2 = px2 * px2
bytes_new = total2 * bpp // 8
print(px)
print(total)
print(bytes_full)
print(px2)
print(total2)
print(bytes_new)

examples.question: A 6 in × 2 in greyscale image is stored at 200 dpi in 8-bit mode. Find its pixel dimensions and uncompressed size.
steps: Width in pixels = 6 in × 200 dpi = 1200 px.
Height in pixels = 2 in × 200 dpi = 400 px.
examples.answer: The image is 1200 × 400 px and 480,000 B (0.48 MB) uncompressed.
examples.check:
w = 6 * 200
h = 2 * 200
print(w)
print(h)
print(w * h)
print(w * h * 8 // 8)

traps: Confusing resample with resize. Lowering dpi alone keeps every pixel, so the file size does not change; resampling throws pixels away and does change it.
Writing dpi as a property of the file's quality. A 1200 × 1200 px image is the same data at 72 dpi and at 300 dpi; only the print size differs.
Mixing up bit depth and colour mode. 24-bit RGB and 8-bit indexed both hold one byte per channel or per palette index, but the indexed image has only 256 colours.
Assuming crop reduces resolution. Crop reduces pixel count and printed size while the dpi value stays as it was.
Using a tight bucket-fill tolerance on a jagged edge and reporting the leftover fringe as a bug in the fill tool; it is the tolerance working as set.

quiz.q: Name the paint tools that change pixels directly.
quiz.a: Brush, airbrush, eraser and bucket fill.

quiz.q: Why does a drawn line stay sharp at 400% zoom while a painted line does not?
quiz.a: The drawn line is stored as endpoints and re-rendered at the new size, so it is computed afresh. The painted line is a fixed grid of pixels that can only be copied and enlarged, so the staircase becomes visible.

quiz.q: A 5 in × 3 in image at 250 dpi in 24-bit colour is resampled to 125 dpi at the same print size. Find the size in bytes before and after.
quiz.a: Before: 1250 × 750 = 937,500 px, × 3 B = 2,812,500 B. After: 625 × 375 = 234,375 px, × 3 B = 703,125 B. The pixel count falls to one quarter.

quiz.q: A designer changes an image from 300 dpi to 72 dpi using the resize option and reports that the file size did not change. Is the tool faulty?
quiz.a: No. Resize only changes the print size, so the pixel grid and the byte count stay the same. Only the printed dimensions grew. To shrink the file, the image must be resampled.

quiz.q: What does the tolerance setting of bucket fill control?
quiz.a: How far a pixel's colour may differ from the clicked pixel and still be included in the flood. Large tolerance fills more area, small tolerance fills less.

quiz.q: Why does upsampling need interpolation, and how do nearest neighbour and bilinear differ?
quiz.a: Upsampling creates new pixel positions that had no value, so a rule must supply one. Nearest neighbour copies the closest original pixel and gives hard blocks; bilinear averages the four surrounding originals and gives smoother, softer output.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production tools now blend the two storage models: a brush stroke in a vector tool is a path that also carries a texture, and a bitmap editor can keep a live text layer. Colour management has moved from per-file guesswork to embedded ICC profiles, so the same numbers look right on a print shop's press and on a phone. Non-destructive editing — adjustment layers and smart filters — is standard in retouching, and generative fill now invents pixels where the editor asks, which makes the resample-versus-resize distinction matter more, not less. Search next for ICC profiles, non-destructive editing and image resampling kernels.
